answer: Traditional African instruments encompass many distinct musical traditions rather than one shared sound. The mbira uses plucked metal tongues, the kora is a plucked string instrument, and the balafon has struck wooden bars. Yoruba dundun drums change pitch through tension cords. Each instrument has specific local names, makers, performance practices and cultural contexts.

facts.fact: The Met describes the nyonganyonga as a lamellaphone with plucked tongues, tuned by sliding their vibrating lengths.
The Met catalogues a Chokwe kisaanji with 18 tongues tuned using wax and dates it to the late nineteenth century.
The Met identifies the kora as a 21-stringed harp associated with Mandé musical traditions of West Africa.
The Met classifies its late-nineteenth-century balafon as a wooden struck-bar idiophone.
The Met documents a twentieth-century Yoruba dundun (iya ilu) as a variable-tension drum.
The Smithsonian describes a talking drum’s pitch changing when the performer squeezes its connecting cords.
